pleiades.blurb: The Pleiades is a nearby cluster of young, hot stars, also called the Seven Sisters.
pleiades.fact: The cluster is only about 100 million years old, far younger than the Sun.

m101.blurb: M101 is the Pinwheel Galaxy, a large spiral galaxy similar in shape to our own.
m101.fact: M101 is roughly twice the width of the Milky Way.

beehive.blurb: The Beehive Cluster (M44) is an open star cluster visible to the naked eye.
beehive.fact: It's one of the nearest open star clusters to the Sun.

ecliptic0.blurb: This field lies in the ecliptic plane, the path the Sun and planets trace across the sky -- where most asteroids orbit too.
ecliptic0.fact: Fields on the ecliptic are where moving solar-system objects are most likely to turn up.

ecliptic180.blurb: This field lies in the ecliptic plane, the path the Sun and planets trace across the sky -- where most asteroids orbit too.
ecliptic180.fact: Fields on the ecliptic are where moving solar-system objects are most likely to turn up.

galactic_center.blurb: This field looks toward the center of the Milky Way galaxy.
galactic_center.fact: The Milky Way's central supermassive black hole, Sagittarius A*, lies in this direction.

north_pole.blurb: This field looks toward the north ecliptic pole, perpendicular to the plane of the solar system.
north_pole.fact: Being far from the ecliptic plane, this region sees very few asteroids or comets passing through.

south_pole.blurb: This field looks toward the south ecliptic pole, perpendicular to the plane of the solar system.
south_pole.fact: Being far from the ecliptic plane, this region sees very few asteroids or comets passing through.
